exercises.objective: Explain why convexity guarantees global optimality of a local minimum.
exercises.prompt: A function $f$ is convex if, for any two points $x_1,x_2$ and $t\in[0,1]$, $f(tx_1+(1-t)x_2) \le t f(x_1)+(1-t)f(x_2)$ (the function lies below the straight line connecting any two of its points). For a general (non-convex) function, a local minimum found by gradient descent or Newton's method might not be the global minimum. Explain why convexity rules this out: why must a local minimum of a convex function also be a global minimum?
hints: Suppose, for contradiction, that $x^*$ is a local minimum but not global: there's some other point $\hat x$ with $f(\hat x) < f(x^*)$.

Consider the straight line segment from $x^*$ to $\hat x$: by convexity, $f$ along this segment lies below (or on) the straight line connecting $f(x^*)$ and $f(\hat x)$. Since $f(\hat x) < f(x^*)$, that straight line is strictly decreasing as you move from $x^*$ toward $\hat x$.

So arbitrarily close to $x^*$ along that segment (small $t$), $f$ must be strictly less than $f(x^*)$, contradicting $x^*$ being a LOCAL minimum (which requires $f(x^*)$ to be the smallest value in some neighborhood around $x^*$). So no such $\hat x$ can exist: every local minimum of a convex function is automatically global.

exercises.objective: Derive the log-barrier gradient and explain its behavior near the constraint boundary.

The log-barrier method replaces an inequality constraint $g(x)\le 0$ with a penalty term added to the objective: $f_t(x) = f(x) - \dfrac{1}{t}\log(-g(x))$, for a parameter $t>0$ (larger $t$ means a weaker barrier). Derive $

$

abla g(x)) = - rac{1}{t\,(-g(x))}
abla g(x)$. Combined with $
abla f(x)$: $
abla_x f_t(x) = 
abla f(x) - \dfrac{1}{t\,g(x)}
abla g(x)$ (note $g(x)<0$ inside the feasible region, so this term is well-defined and finite there).

As $x$ approaches the boundary, $g(x)\to 0^-$, so $\dfrac{1}{t\,g(x)} \to -\infty$ (a large negative number divided by a small negative number), meaning the barrier's gradient contribution grows without bound. This is exactly the intended behavior: it creates an increasingly strong 'repulsive force' pushing $x$ back into the strict interior as it approaches the boundary, which is why the log-barrier method never actually reaches an infeasible point despite operating on an unconstrained problem.

exercises.objective: Recognize and write a problem in standard LP form.
exercises.prompt: A linear program (LP) in standard form is $\min_x c^\top x$ s.t. $Ax\le b$ (linear objective, linear inequality constraints). Consider: $\max_x (2x_1+3x_2)$ s.t. $x_1+x_2\le 10$, $x_1\ge0$, $x_2\ge0$. Rewrite this as a standard-form LP (i.e. as a minimization with $Ax\le b$), being explicit about how you handle the fact that it's originally a maximization and that $x_1\ge0,x_2\ge0$ are also inequality constraints that need to fit the $Ax\le b$ pattern.
hints: Maximizing $c^\top x$ is the same as minimizing $-c^\top x$: so the objective becomes $\min_x (-2x_1-3x_2)$.
$x_1\ge 0$ needs to be rewritten in the $\le$ form to fit the pattern: $-x_1 \le 0$. Similarly $x_2\ge0$ becomes $-x_2\le0$.

Full standard form: $c=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-3\end{pmatrix}$, $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\-1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$, $b=\begin{pmatrix}10\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}$, i.e. $\min_x c^\top x$ s.t. $Ax\le b$ with these three stacked inequality rows.
